% Auto-generated by thesis/make_prompts.py --- do not edit by hand.
% Source: analyse_ofsted_reports.py, analyse_behaviour_policies_v3.py

Both scorers share a prompt architecture. A system instruction establishes
the task, the scoring procedure and the output contract; the substantive
content is delivered as a single JSON payload carrying the school
identifiers, the extracted document text, the full rubric, and a
specification of the required output fields. The model must return
schema-valid JSON --- through the provider's structured-output facility
where available, and through a forced tool call otherwise --- so that no
free-text parsing is involved. Sampling temperature is zero. Each request is
keyed by a SHA-256 hash of the model name, prompt version, schema version and
payload, so re-running a scorer over unchanged documents returns cached
scores rather than silently re-scoring them.

Both rubrics require the model to state, for every score, why the score is
not one point higher and not one point lower. Both apply the same borderline
rule: where evidence is genuinely ambiguous, the lower score is taken. The
asymmetric exception in both is that a score below the midpoint requires
positive evidence of a deficiency --- silence on behaviour, or on
relationships, is scored as unremarkable rather than as poor. This matters
for interpreting the warmth null in \cref{sec:p1_text_valid}: the rubrics are
constructed so that a document which simply does not discuss warmth cannot
produce a low warmth score, and the observed compression at the midpoint is
therefore the designed response to silence, not a scoring failure.

\subsection*{Ofsted reports}

Prompt version \texttt{ofsted-strictness-warmth-teaching-v3}. System instruction:

\begin{quote}\small
You are scoring Ofsted report evidence for research. Use only the supplied passages and rubric. Apply the hard rules exactly. You must call the record\_scores tool with your scores --- do not reply in plain text.
\end{quote}

The payload supplies the URN and school name, the inspection date, the
report type with any stated grade removed from its wording, and the
grade-stripped uniform report body: the substantive inspection narrative
with boilerplate, primary-phase and sixth-form-specific passages removed
and every stated grade deleted, so that no field available to the model
carries the inspection verdict. For an
all-through school a further note instructs the model to score only the
secondary provision described in the remaining text. The required output is a
score, a confidence level and a reason for each of strictness, warmth and
teaching, plus a manual-review flag.

\paragraph{Strictness scale anchors}
\begin{description}
\item[Score 1] Rules are unclear, inconsistently applied, or disruption is a persistent and documented problem.
\item[Score 2] Standards exist but enforcement is patchy --- some year groups, subjects, or staff are exceptions; behaviour is an identified area for improvement. Note: Ofsted inspections take place when schools are typically presenting their best behaviour --- pupils and staff are aware they are being observed. Direct observations by inspectors of low-level disruption, inattention, or inconsistent enforcement during the visit therefore carry more evidential weight than they might appear to, and should weigh toward S=2 rather than S=3 even if described mildly.
\item[Score 3] Clear expectations are in place and generally maintained; the evidence mentions behaviour or conduct but without singling it out as a strength. Adequate, unremarkable enforcement.
\item[Score 4] Multiple evidence passages consistently indicate that conduct standards are above average --- the evidence as a whole suggests behaviour is a strength, with adults clearly driving high expectations. Does not require verbatim ``strength'' language but the pattern across passages must clearly point above adequate. If behaviour outside the classroom --- corridors, social times, around the building --- is explicitly flagged as an improvement area, this prevents a 4; above-average conduct must be consistent across the whole school environment, not just in lessons.
\item[Score 5] The evidence emphatically and consistently highlights conduct as exceptional across most or all passages --- the school's strictness is unmistakably a defining feature of its character.
\end{description}

\paragraph{Warmth scale anchors}
\begin{description}
\item[Score 1] Staff-pupil relationships are poor, transactional, or pupils feel unknown or uncared for by staff.
\item[Score 2] The report contains positive evidence of relational inconsistency: some pupils feel unknown to, disconnected from, or let down by staff. Even mild or qualified negative relational language --- pupils feeling their concerns are not always heard, that bullying is not resolved, or that staff are not accessible --- is sufficient for W=2 and is not offset by generic positive language about safety or pastoral provision.
\item[Score 3] The report describes a safe and generally positive environment. Positive language is present but it characterises the school's overall character or provision rather than the quality of actual staff-pupil interactions. W=3 language: the school described as ``calm'', ``caring'', ``warm'', ``welcoming'', or ``inclusive'' used as a general school-level label; pupils feeling safe, happy, settled, or supported stated as an outcome without describing how staff create that; generic statements that staff are supportive, approachable, or accessible (availability, not relational quality); PSHE, pastoral teams, heads of year, or trusted-adult arrangements mentioned or described positively; enrichment activities or school events. None of these describe relational quality --- they describe provision, character labels, or bare outcomes. Note: any credible negative relational signal --- pupils feeling bullying is not resolved, that they do not feel safe, or that staff are not available --- should pull the score toward W=2.
\item[Score 4] The evidence describes the quality of staff-pupil relationships in explicit terms that go beyond characterising the school's overall character or stating that systems exist. W=4 language describes HOW staff and pupils actually relate --- not just that a warm school exists or that pastoral provision is in place. Qualifying language includes: staff described as knowing pupils well; inspectors observing or describing warm, caring, or positive interactions between staff and pupils; strong, warm, or positive staff-pupil relationships described as a characteristic of how adults and pupils interact (not merely as a school-label adjective); pupils described as feeling genuinely valued, known, or cared for in ways that attribute this to staff behaviour or the relational quality rather than to provision existing; staff described as caring about pupils as individuals; pupils having positive or trusting relationships with staff. DOES NOT QUALIFY for W=4 (stays at W=3): ``caring school'', ``warm community'', ``inclusive ethos'', ``staff are approachable / accessible'', ``pupils can speak to a trusted adult'', ``pastoral team is effective'', ``bullying is dealt with swiftly'', ``PSHE is taught well'', ``there is a positive school community''. These are provision-existence or school-character statements, not descriptions of relational quality. No significant relational negatives are present. Where both positive and negative relational evidence appear, the score is W=3.
\item[Score 5] Relational warmth is a prominent and explicitly named feature of the school's character, evidenced across multiple passages. To reach W=5, warmth or the quality of staff-pupil relationships must be described as a standout, defining, or exceptional feature of the school --- not merely present or adequate. Markers: inspectors use language such as ``exceptionally caring'', ``deeply supportive'', ``truly know their pupils'', ``outstanding relationships'', or equivalent; multiple passages independently converge on the same positive relational theme; or warmth is explicitly named as one of the school's defining characteristics. A single warm passage alongside generic positives does not reach W=5. The absence of negatives alone is never sufficient --- positive evidence of distinctive relational quality must be present.
\end{description}

\paragraph{Scoring rules: strictness and warmth}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Use only the supplied evidence.
\item Do not infer beyond the supplied evidence.
\item The Ofsted Behaviour and attitudes judgement is provided as context only; do not treat it as a hard cap on your score.
\item BORDERLINE RULE: When evidence is genuinely ambiguous or limited, always assign the lower score. For scores that sit on the boundary between two adjacent values --- where reasonable arguments exist for both --- always choose the lower value. A higher score is warranted only when the evidence clearly and unambiguously supports it. This is a deliberate design choice for consistency. IMPORTANT EXCEPTION FOR STRICTNESS: scores of 1 or 2 each require positive evidence that behavioural problems exist (documented disruption, patchy enforcement, behaviour identified as an improvement area). If behaviour is simply not discussed in the report --- because the overall picture is positive and inspectors focused elsewhere --- do not score below 3. Absence of behaviour-focused writing is not evidence of poor behaviour; default to 3 (adequate, unremarkable) in that case. IMPORTANT EXCEPTION FOR WARMTH: scores of 1 or 2 each require positive evidence of poor or absent staff-pupil relationships --- explicit descriptions of pupils feeling uncared for, unknown to staff, or unsafe due to relational failures, or of staff-pupil relationships being poor or transactional. If warmth is simply not discussed in the report --- because inspectors focused on curriculum, outcomes, or other aspects --- do not score below 3. Absence of warmth-focused writing is not evidence of poor warmth; default to 3 (safe and generally positive, no direct relational description) in that case.
\item For each final score, explain briefly why the score is not one point higher and not one point lower.
\item PUPIL VIEWS ON RULES ARE WARMTH EVIDENCE ONLY: How pupils perceive, accept, or resent the school's rules and strictness must feed exclusively into the warmth score and must have no effect on the strictness score in any direction --- it must not raise it, lower it, or prevent it from reaching any threshold, including 5. Strictness is scored solely on what adults do: the standards they set, how consistently they enforce them, and the resulting behavioural outcomes. Whether pupils welcome or resent those standards is a relational question, not a strictness question. If you find yourself citing pupil views about rules as a reason to withhold a strictness score of 5, you are violating this rule --- remove that reasoning and re-evaluate based only on what the adults do.
\item WARMTH EXCLUSION (NARROW): SEND provision, knowledge of individual educational needs, mental health promotion programmes, and specialist provision for vulnerable groups are NOT evidence of warmth. General pastoral systems (e.g. trusted adults, pastoral teams described as accessible to all pupils), PSHE/PSHCE programmes, and whole-school care structures CAN be counted as warmth evidence --- but their existence qualifies only for W=3. Warmth is primarily evidenced by descriptions of the relational quality between staff and pupils: explicit kindness language, staff caring for pupils as individuals, pupils feeling genuinely valued and respected, gratitude practices, or direct statements that staff have pupils' best interests at heart.
\item W=3/W=4 THRESHOLD --- RELATIONAL QUALITY VS PROVISION OR CHARACTER LABEL: The most common scoring error is treating positive language about the school's general character or systems as evidence of relational warmth. The test is: does the evidence describe HOW staff and pupils actually relate --- or does it describe the school's general character, what provision exists, or aggregate outcomes without attributing them to relational quality? STAYS AT W=3: ``calm and caring school'' / ``warm and welcoming'' (school-level label); ``pupils feel safe and happy'' (bare outcome); ``staff are supportive / accessible / approachable'' (availability, not relational quality); ``bullying is dealt with effectively''; ``PSHE is in place''; ``pastoral team / heads of year are effective''; ``there is a positive school community''; ``pupils trust staff to resolve concerns''. QUALIFIES FOR W=4: ``staff know pupils well''; ``strong / warm / positive staff-pupil relationships'' (describing the relationship itself, not a school label); ``inspectors observed warm or caring interactions between staff and pupils''; ``pupils feel genuinely valued and known by staff''; ``staff care about pupils as individuals''; ``pupils have positive, trusting relationships with staff''; ``mutual respect between staff and pupils''. The test is whether the language characterises the relational quality itself --- not just the school's overall tone or what provision is available.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Teaching scale anchors}
\begin{description}
\item[Score 1] Seriously weak teaching, directly harming learning. The report explicitly names teaching quality as a serious failure. Key markers: teacher subject knowledge is described as varying greatly or extremely weak in places; explanations and classroom delivery are described as failing to give pupils the knowledge they need (``work does not enable pupils to gain the knowledge needed for future success''); there is no effective checking of understanding. Outcome language attributes weak results directly to teaching failure (``pupils ill-prepared'', ``many do not receive an acceptable standard of education'', ``achievement is weak''). The picture across the report is one of teaching as a root cause of poor outcomes, not merely a symptom.
\item[Score 2] Inconsistent or developing teaching, named as requiring improvement. Teaching delivers the curriculum in some classrooms but not consistently. Key markers: 'some teachers deliver content clearly... this is not always the case'; checking for understanding is incomplete or ineffective (``do not always check before moving on'', ``feedback not as helpful as it could be'', ``gaps in pupils'' knowledge not addressed swiftly'); teacher adaptation is named as inconsistent (``some staff do not adjust their teaching in response to checks''). Teaching quality is named explicitly as an area requiring improvement. Outcome language describes pupils as ``not achieving as well as they should''. The report may acknowledge pockets of effective practice but the prevailing picture is inconsistency.
\item[Score 3] Adequate and broadly effective. DEFAULT score. Teaching is broadly adequate: the curriculum is delivered competently, teachers have secure subject knowledge, some checking for understanding takes place. Teaching quality is neither praised as a strength nor named as a weakness --- it is either unremarkable or discussed only in terms of curriculum design and sequencing rather than classroom delivery. Pupils make broadly expected progress. DEFAULT: If the report does not specifically discuss how teachers teach in the classroom --- because inspectors focused on curriculum intent, leadership, or behaviour --- assign score 3. Absence of teaching-focused writing is not evidence of poor teaching.
\item[Score 4] Strong classroom teaching, described positively across most of the school. The report describes teaching positively and with some specificity. Key markers: teachers have ``strong subject knowledge'' and ``know how best to share it''; checking for understanding is consistent (``teachers systematically check pupils'' understanding', ``misconceptions are quickly addressed''); teaching is effective for most pupils including those with SEND (``teachers meet needs securely in lessons''); explanations are described as clear and effective. The word ``typically'' or ``most teachers'' appears alongside positive teaching descriptions. Outcomes are good. The report may note isolated inconsistencies but the overall picture of classroom delivery is clearly positive.
\item[Score 5] Expert teaching, consistently described as a school strength. Teaching is described as expert or excellent and as a defining quality of the school. Key markers: ``expert teachers'', ``excellent knowledge''; language of precision and responsiveness (``explain complex ideas very well'', ``deliver subject content with precision'', ``nimble and responsive in adjusting teaching'', ``intervene quickly to address any misconceptions''); formative assessment is systematic and sharp (``teachers check understanding regularly'', ``assessment sharply identifies areas for improvement'', ``precisely tailored adaptations''); ``consistently'' or ``across all subjects'' accompanies praise for teaching. Outcome language explicitly and emphatically attributes strong results to teaching quality. The report leaves no doubt that teaching is an exceptional strength.
\end{description}

\paragraph{Scoring rules: teaching}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Use only the supplied evidence. Do not infer beyond what the report states.
\item DELIVERY vs DESIGN: Curriculum design language (intent, sequencing, what is taught) is background --- not itself evidence of teaching quality. Score only on language about HOW teachers teach in classrooms: subject knowledge, explanations, checking for understanding, adaptation to pupils, and response to gaps or misconceptions. Exception: ``curriculum delivery'' statements that describe what teachers actually do in practice (e.g. ``teachers deliver subject content with precision'') do count as delivery evidence.
\item CONSISTENCY LANGUAGE: Weigh consistency modifiers heavily. ``Consistently / routinely / across all subjects'' alongside positive language $\rightarrow$ push toward 5. ``Typically / most teachers'' with positive language $\rightarrow$ push toward 4. ``Some teachers / not always / inconsistent'' $\rightarrow$ push toward 2-3. ``Many do not / often ineffective'' $\rightarrow$ push toward 1-2.
\item CHECKING FOR UNDERSTANDING is the most reliably graded marker in Ofsted reports. If checking is described as sharp, precise, and responsive $\rightarrow$ supports 4-5. If described as present but incomplete or slow $\rightarrow$ supports 3-4. If described as absent, ineffective, or not acted on $\rightarrow$ supports 1-2.
\item BORDERLINE RULE: When delivery evidence is genuinely limited or absent, default to 3. When evidence points between two scores, prefer the lower unless outcome language explicitly and emphatically credits teaching quality.
\item For the final teaching score, explain briefly why it is not one point higher and not one point lower.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Behaviour policy documents}

Prompt version \texttt{behaviour-policy-strictness-warmth-v26}. The system instruction
carries the scoring procedure itself, as an explicit decision tree rather than
as holistic guidance:

\begin{quote}\small
You are scoring school behaviour policy evidence for academic research. Use the anchor examples in the rubric as calibration references. Score strictness and warmth independently.

STRICTNESS DECISION PROCEDURE --- follow these steps in order:

Step 1: Does the policy describe a day-to-day detention or consequence system? (Not merely mentioning detentions exist; not merely listing what offences lead to suspension or permanent exclusion.) If NO --- score S=1 or S=2. S=1 = no consequence language at all (empty policy, rewards-only, purely aspirational with no sanctions content). S=2 = some consequence language is present but no coherent day-to-day system is described --- this includes policies with vague/proportionate sanctions language, restorative-primary approaches, or exclusions-only content.

Step 2 (only if Step 1 = YES): Is there a named tracking system (demerits, BfL points) with explicit numeric thresholds that automatically generate a named consequence? If NO --- score S=3. If YES --- go to Step 3.

Step 3 (only if Step 2 = YES): Does the demerit trigger list include ANY of: posture or seating position; eye contact/tracking/SLANTing; written work neatness or quality; corridor conduct (wrong side, running); minor uniform details (untucked shirt, incorrect shoe)? Note: qualifiers such as ``persistently'', ``repeatedly'', or ``sloppy'' specify the INFRACTION THRESHOLD, not whether staff choose to sanction --- they do NOT introduce discretion. If YES --- score S=5. If NO --- score S=4.

WARMTH DECISION PROCEDURE --- follow these steps in order:

Step 1: Does the policy contain positive culture content BEYOND aspirational sentences that describe the school's VALUES or EMPHASIS without naming any mechanism? The following do NOT count regardless of how elaborate they are: ``Emphasis is on recognising and celebrating effort and success so that all members feel valued and rewarded''; ``We develop all pupils in the habits of self-discipline and kindness''; ``students who behave well are likely to receive a reward''; any sentence describing what the school VALUES about recognition, success, or positive culture without naming specific rewards, pastoral structures, or staff practices. The following DO count: named rewards (house points, certificates, commendation events); named pastoral services (counselling, SEMH, safe spaces, pastoral programmes); explicit HOW-to staff guidance (operational, not aspirational). If NO qualifying content $\rightarrow$ W=1 [STOP --- do not proceed further]. If YES $\rightarrow$ Step 2.

Step 2a --- REWARDS CHECK: Does the policy describe a NAMED rewards mechanism with named types (house points, certificates, commendation events, reward tokens) AND described occasions? If YES $\rightarrow$ Step 2b. If NO $\rightarrow$ Step 2c.

Step 2b (rewards present) --- INDEPENDENT PASTORAL CHECK: Are there also INDEPENDENTLY ACCESSIBLE pastoral/wellbeing structures --- counselling service, SEMH lead, wellbeing programme, safe space available to ALL students independent of sanction status, dedicated pastoral programme? NON-QUALIFYING (consequence-integrated only): HoY/SLT reports for sanctioned students, homework clubs for non-compliant students, reintegration meetings after removal, restorative conversations within the consequence procedure, self-control mentoring triggered by poor behaviour, support strategies mentioned in exclusion procedure text. If YES independent pastoral $\rightarrow$ Step 3. If NO independent pastoral $\rightarrow$ W=3.

Step 2c (NO rewards) --- INDEPENDENT PASTORAL CHECK: Are there INDEPENDENTLY ACCESSIBLE pastoral/wellbeing structures (counselling, SEMH, wellbeing programme, non-consequence-triggered safe spaces --- as defined above)? If YES $\rightarrow$ W=3 [STOP --- do not proceed to Step 3]. If NO $\rightarrow$ W=2 [STOP --- do not proceed to Step 3]. (Consequence-integrated supports alone, however numerous, cannot exceed W=2.)

Step 3: Is there explicit operational guidance on HOW staff should relate to individual students --- instructional (``learn their names'', ``use humour --- it builds bridges'', ``know your students as individuals''), not merely aspirational (``be positive'', ``be kind'')? If YES $\rightarrow$ W=4. If NO $\rightarrow$ W=3.

Your reasons must cite specific features from the policy text and explain why the chosen score is not one point higher or lower. CRITICAL: You may ONLY cite text that appears in the policy\_text field of this prompt. Do NOT reproduce or quote text from the rubric anchor descriptions as if it were evidence from the policy being scored. Anchor descriptions are calibration references --- citing them as if they appear in the current policy is fabrication and will produce wrong scores. Return only schema-valid JSON.
\end{quote}

The payload supplies the URN, school name and the title of the selected
document; a set of keyword-matched passages, explicitly labelled as
preliminary signals to be checked against the full text rather than scored on
directly; a flag and term list recording whether specialist-support vocabulary
is present; and the extracted policy text. The required output is a score, a
confidence level and a reason for each of strictness and warmth, plus a
manual-review flag.

\paragraph{Strictness scale anchors}
\begin{description}
\item[Score 1] No consequence language of any kind. The policy is empty, consists entirely of rewards and recognition content, or is so aspirational that no sanctions, detentions, or consequences are described or even implied. Purely aspirational statements about values, culture, or the importance of good behaviour are S=1 if unaccompanied by any consequence content whatsoever.
\item[Score 2] Consequence language is present but no coherent day-to-day system is described. Three common forms: (a) proportionate or contextual sanctions are mentioned without describing when, how, or by whom they are applied; (b) a restorative or relational approach is the primary framework and sanctions appear only as a last resort; (c) the only consequence content is an exclusions/suspensions procedure with no working day-to-day system described alongside it. Key test: could a new member of staff read this policy and know what to do tomorrow when a student disrupts a lesson? If not, it is S=2 (assuming some consequence language is present --- otherwise S=1).
\item[Score 3] A working detentions and isolation system with a clear rules framework. Staff apply consequences by judgment from a menu of options --- no named tracking system, no automatic thresholds. Language such as ``sanctions may include'' and ``at the discretion of staff'' throughout. This is the standard English secondary behaviour policy.
\item[Score 4] A named tracking system where consequence type is determined automatically by position in the system, removing staff discretion over WHICH consequence follows. Two qualifying forms: (a) POINT-ACCUMULATION --- named demerit or BfL points reach a numeric threshold that automatically triggers a named consequence (e.g. ``4 demerits $\rightarrow$ 60-minute detention''); (b) TIERED EVENT-ESCALATION --- named consequence tiers (e.g. C1/C2/C3, Level 1/2/3) where each tier automatically produces a defined sanction (e.g. 'C1 = verbal warning recorded; C2 = same-day detention; C3 = removal to [named facility]'). Form (b) does NOT require a numeric point total --- the tier itself is the decision mechanism. Key test: once a threshold is crossed or a tier is invoked, is the consequence determined by the system position, or by staff judgment at that moment? If the former, S=4. If staff are still choosing from a menu of possible consequences at the point of issue, S=3. Staff may retain discretion over whether to initiate the first action, but not over which consequence the system then generates. Skipping to a higher tier for a more serious incident is severity calibration within S=4, not evidence of discretion over whether to use the system.
\item[Score 5] S=4 baseline, plus two additional features that must BOTH be present: (1) MANDATORY issuance --- the staff member has no discretion at the trigger point (``a demerit is given if a pupil does X'', not ``staff may give a demerit''); AND (2) triggers include continuous IN-LESSON DEPORTMENT NORMS --- always-on conduct standards actively monitored throughout lessons, such as posture/SLANT, eye contact/tracking the teacher, or corridor deportment. WHAT DOES NOT QUALIFY as a deportment-norm trigger for criterion (2): --- Demerit CATEGORY LABELS such as ``Line up conduct'', ``Uniform'', ``Equipment'', ``Transition conduct'' name violation types, not conduct surveillance standards. A list of category labels without accompanying mandatory-issuance language is a category taxonomy --- S=4 maximum. --- Classroom procedural transitions (standing behind chair, lining up) are classroom procedures, not ambient conduct norms --- they do not qualify. --- A stepped-warning process (e.g. reminder $\rightarrow$ verbal warning $\rightarrow$ demerit at step 3) makes issuance discretionary, capping at S=4 regardless of what the category list contains. Score S=5 ONLY when both mandatory issuance AND genuine deportment-norm triggers (posture, SLANT, eye contact) are unambiguously present in the text.
\end{description}

\paragraph{Warmth scale anchors}
\begin{description}
\item[Score 1] No described positive culture infrastructure. The policy may contain an aspirational sentence about values or mention that good behaviour earns a reward, but no reward system is named, no pastoral structures are described, and no relational language about how staff and students interact is present.
\item[Score 2] Aspirational values or ethos language is present (dignity, respect, kindness) but the policy is operationally consequence-dominated. Positive elements exist in name only: rewards mentioned but not described, pastoral support referenced but not structured, relational language generic and aspirational rather than operational.
\item[Score 3] A described rewards system (house points, certificates, commendations, positive contact home) and reference to pastoral support structures. The positive culture section is functional --- processes and systems are named --- but staff-student relational quality is not characterised. This is the standard English secondary policy warmth level.
\item[Score 4] Both of the following clearly present --- these two criteria are necessary AND sufficient. Nothing else is required: (1) a named, described reward system with occasions or criteria; (2) explicit operational guidance on HOW staff should relate to individual students --- instructional rather than aspirational (e.g. ``learn their names'', ``use humour to build bridges'', ``know your students as individuals'', de-escalation scripts, greeting strategies). SCORING RULE: If BOTH criteria are clearly present, assign W=4. Do not require any third criterion. IMPORTANT --- WHAT IS IRRELEVANT TO THIS DECISION: Pastoral support structures (Heads of Year, form tutors, wellbeing teams, safeguarding leads) appear in the W=3 descriptor but play NO role in the W=4 decision. Do not use their presence or absence to determine this score. A school with criterion (1) AND criterion (2) scores W=4 even if no pastoral structures are described.
\item[Score 5] W=4 criteria met, plus the policy explicitly characterises the relational culture --- naming warmth, care, or belonging as values and describing the quality of the staff-student relationship itself, not just what staff should do operationally. This goes beyond tips or instructions into describing how staff and students actually relate (e.g. ``staff know and invest in pupils as individuals'', ``relationships of care and trust underpin how we respond to behaviour''). The positive culture content is substantial and prominently placed in the document, not confined to a brief introduction or appendix.
\end{description}

\paragraph{Scoring rules}
\begin{enumerate}
\item SCORE INDEPENDENTLY: Strictness and warmth are not opposites --- a policy can be high on both or low on both. Score each dimension on its own evidence.
\item MENTION $\neq$ DESCRIBED SYSTEM: The words ``detention'', ``sanction'', or ``reward'' in the text do not mean a described system exists. A described sanctions system explains when consequences are applied, by whom, and the procedure. A described reward system names what rewards exist and how they are given. Do not default to S=3 or W=3 simply because the words appear.
\item EXCLUSION PROCEDURES ARE NOT A SANCTIONS SYSTEM: A policy whose main body describes what offences lead to suspension or permanent exclusion is not a day-to-day behaviour management system. Detailed exclusion procedure text --- even spanning multiple pages --- is consistent with S=2 if no working day-to-day consequence system is described alongside it.
\item S=3 IS NOT THE UNCERTAINTY DEFAULT: S=3 must be earned with a described working detention system. If your reasoning concludes no day-to-day system is described, score S=1 or S=2 --- not S=3 because the evidence is thin.
\item S=4/5 BOUNDARY --- DISCRETION AT THE TRIGGER: S=4 removes discretion over WHICH consequence follows a threshold or tier. S=5 additionally requires that initiating a consequence is MANDATORY at the trigger point (not a choice the staff member makes), AND that triggers include continuous in-lesson deportment norms. Standard rule compliance violations listed as demerit categories --- uniform infringement, equipment, lateness --- do NOT qualify as deportment-norm triggers for S=5. They must be part of an always-on conduct surveillance system explicitly enforced alongside posture/tracking norms to qualify. Classroom procedural transitions (standing behind chair, lining up) do not qualify. Language test: ``a demerit is given if a pupil [does X]'' is mandatory (S=5 possible); ``staff may give a demerit if a pupil [does X]'' is discretionary (S=4 maximum). A plain list of demerit category labels (e.g. ``L1 - Demerit - Uniform''; ``L1 - Demerit - Transition conduct'') without accompanying mandatory-issuance language is a category taxonomy, not a mandatory trigger --- treat as discretionary (S=4 maximum). Similarly, a stepped-warning process (e.g. reminder $\rightarrow$ verbal warning $\rightarrow$ demerit at step 3) means initiation is discretionary even if the demerit category list includes conduct-related items. S=4 consequences are for rule violations (lateness, equipment, uniform, disruption); S=5 additionally covers ambient conduct norms monitored continuously in lessons --- posture, SLANT, eye contact, tracking the teacher. Demerit category labels such as ``Line up conduct'', ``Uniform'', or ``Equipment'' name violation types, not conduct surveillance standards.
\item W=4 REQUIRES BOTH AND ONLY BOTH: The two W=4 criteria (described reward system; operational staff guidance on relating to students as individuals) are jointly necessary and sufficient. If both are clearly present, score W=4. If either is clearly absent, the maximum is W=3. Do NOT treat pastoral support structures as a prerequisite for W=4 --- they appear in the W=3 descriptor but are irrelevant to the W=4 decision. A school with criterion (1) and criterion (2) clearly met scores W=4 even if no independent pastoral structures are described.
\item WARMTH EXCLUSIONS: SEND provision, mental health promotion programmes, safeguarding, and therapeutic interventions do not count toward warmth.
\item SCORE PRIMARY EMPHASIS: Do not reward incidental language. Score what the policy devotes its attention to --- restorative language buried in a consequence-heavy policy does not raise the warmth score; a brief positive section in an otherwise sanctions-focused document does not raise the score.
\item DO NOT REWARD LENGTH: A longer policy does not earn a higher score. Score on the intensity, specificity, and centrality of the evidence.
\item Use only the supplied evidence. Do not infer beyond the text.
\item BORDERLINE $\rightarrow$ LOWER SCORE: When evidence could support two adjacent scores, assign the lower. The distinguishing feature of the higher score must be clearly and unambiguously present.
\item EXPLAIN ADJACENT SCORES: For each score, briefly explain why it is not one point higher and not one point lower.
\end{enumerate}

A second behaviour-policy instrument (prompt version
\texttt{behaviour-policy-strictness-warmth-v28-fulltext}) is used for the
robustness columns in \cref{ch:paper2}. It reads the full policy text
rather than an extract and carries revised threshold anchors; its rules
follow the same form as those above and are in
\texttt{analyse\_behaviour\_policies\_v4.py}.

\subsection*{The decomposed instruments}

The website and interview instruments do not ask the model for a band.
Each asks a fixed set of factual questions about one document; every
affirmative answer must be supported by a verbatim quotation, which is
checked against the document before it counts; and the band is assigned
by a fixed rule in ordinary code. For concision, the question texts and
banding rules are reproduced here in their operative form; each
instrument also carries exclusion clauses (what does not count) and
tie-break rules, which are stated in full in its scoring script in the
project repository.

\subsection*{Website warmth}

Prompt version \texttt{website-warmth-v18r2-counted-referent-floor}. Construct:
WARMTH here is HOW BROAD AND HOW DEEP a relational commitment the school makes, on its own website, about how its pupils are cared for and known. You are describing what the school has chosen to put in writing about the relationships inside it --- not whether the school is in fact a warm place, not whether its pupils are happy, and not whether it is a good school. The relationship that matters is the one between the SCHOOL'S ADULTS and ITS PUPILS. Relationships with parents, with the local community, with neighbours, with employers, with feeder primaries or between one school and another in a trust are a different subject and do not answer these questions. The distinction that runs through the whole instrument is between ASSERTING and DESCRIBING. Almost every school website in the country says it cares about its pupils; far fewer describe an arrangement, a role, a routine or a manner through which that care is delivered. Several questions below turn on which of the two the site is doing. One item asks you to LIST sentences rather than answer true or false; its own instructions govern it. Each question asks about ONE thing and is answered on its own.

\paragraph{The questions}
\begin{enumerate}\small
\item \textit{relational claim recurs.} Does the relational claim COME BACK, rather than appearing once and being dropped? Answer true where a statement passing the relational referent test appears on more than one of the crawled pages, or more than once on a single page. The crawl is only ever about three pages, so two of them is most of what can be seen, and the identical sentence on two pages does count. Answer FALSE where the repetition is template furniture that rides on every page regardless of its content --- a navigation menu, a breadcrumb, a sidebar, a footer or a banner strapline. Answer false if the relational referent test is not passed at all.
\item \textit{relational claim intensified.} Is the relational claim PRESSED, rather than mentioned in passing? Answer true where a statement passing the relational referent test is given a sentence or more of its own, is made the school's defining idea, or is stated as a commitment the school organises itself around --- as opposed to sitting as one item in a list of values, one adjective in a strapline, or a subordinate clause inside a sentence about something else. Raising the adjective does not intensify anything: a school whose staff are deeply and profoundly committed to knowing pupils has gone no further than one whose staff know them. Answer false if the relational referent test is not passed at all.
\item \textit{route to a person described.} Does the site describe HOW A PUPIL REACHES AN ADULT? Answer true where a pastoral or tutorial arrangement is described in terms of who a particular pupil's adult is, when or how often they see them, in what size of group, or what happens when a pupil needs someone. The test is that you could picture a particular child getting to a particular adult. NAMING THAT AN ARRANGEMENT EXISTS IS NOT DESCRIBING IT: a house system, a form group, a tutor for every pupil, a head of year, a pastoral team or a wellbeing team, named and left there, is a naming and answers this question FALSE. The distinguishing mark is that something in the sentence would have to be DIFFERENT at another school.
\item \textit{named relational practice.} Does the site describe a RECURRING THING THE ADULTS DO in order to know their pupils --- a coaching, check-in, key-adult or mentoring arrangement --- given with enough of its working that it is an account rather than a label? Answer false where the practice is only named. Answer false for support SERVICES described as services, which is provision rather than relationship: counselling, mental-health referral, SEND provision, a wellbeing team, an alternative provision. Answer false for enrichment, clubs, trips and house competitions, however warmly described.
\item \textit{described availability.} Does the site describe a WAY IN WHICH ADULTS ARE REACHABLE by pupils --- a named adult whose job is to be available, together with what a pupil can go to them for, or a described time or place at which pupils can find staff? Answer FALSE for the bare claim that staff are approachable, friendly, always there or have an open door, which asserts availability rather than describing it.
\item \textit{pupil voice about staff.} Does a PUPIL, STUDENT OR FORMER PUPIL speak in their own words about being known, valued, cared for or supported BY THE SCHOOL'S ADULTS? The voice must be about the adults. Answer FALSE where a pupil quotation is about opportunities, facilities, clubs, friendships, how much they have achieved or how much they enjoy the school --- that is testimony about the provision, not about a relationship. Quotation carousels are common on this corpus and most of their contents fail this question.
\item \textit{narrated particular.} Does the site NARRATE A PARTICULAR OCCASION on which adults invested in an identifiable pupil or group as people --- with enough detail that it happened once, rather than that it happens generally? Answer FALSE for a general practice written in the present tense. Answer FALSE for news and social-media items celebrating a pupil's achievement, an awards evening, a concert, a sports result or a trip: congratulating a pupil for succeeding is not an account of an adult investing in them as a person.
\item \textit{parent witness to staff action.} Does a PARENT describe, in their own words, something the school's adults DID for their child? The account must name an action the adults took. Answer FALSE for generic parental praise --- thanking the school, saying how proud they are, saying their child is happy or settled, recommending the school. That is testimonial rather than an instance. Note that the school's partnership with families as a TOPIC is excluded everywhere else in this instrument; this question is the single place a parent's words are evidence, and only as a WITNESS to what staff did for a pupil.
\item \textit{neg school presents itself through results.} Is the school's account OF ITSELF built on outcomes, selection, standards or facilities, with care and relationships subordinate to that or absent? This is a question about the WHOLE crawl and its centre of gravity, not about whether achievement is mentioned --- almost every site mentions it. Answer true where the site introduces and explains the school principally through its examination results, its league table position, its selective or grammar status, its Ofsted grade, its destinations and university places, its academic reputation, or its buildings and facilities, and where relational or pastoral material is thin, late or missing beside that. Answer FALSE where results and care are both given real weight, and false where the site is simply short or thin rather than achievement-forward. A school can be proud of its results and still answer this false.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{The banding rule}
A site with no verified relational referent is band 1; one or more verified referents reach band 2; a claim that recurs or is intensified reaches band 3; a described arrangement (a route to a named person, a named relational practice, described availability) reaches band 4; a narrated instance, pupil voice, or a parent witnessed account reaches band 5. The highest finding wins, and a site that presents itself principally through results is capped.

The instrument additionally carries 10 exclusion clauses and 8 hard rules, stated in full in \texttt{score\_website\_warmth\_v18.py}.

\subsection*{Website strictness}

Prompt version \texttt{website-strictness-v13-four-band-climate-word-tightened}. Construct:
You are reading a crawl of a school's own public website --- typically its homepage, its values or ethos page and its welcome page. Three pages is all there is. STRICTNESS is HOW FAR THE SCHOOL GOES in what it publishes about pupil conduct: does it name conduct itself and require it of pupils, reaching small specific things and the consequences attached to them --- or does it stop at value words? THE CONSTRUCT IS GRANULARITY AND SPECIFICITY, NOT SEVERITY. A school describing a warm, restorative approach in concrete detail scores HIGHER than one that says ``we have high expectations'' and nothing else. Do not reward harshness and do not penalise kindness; reward detail. This is the school's own voice. You are recording what the school SAYS, not whether it is strict, not whether it enforces anything, and not whether it is a good school. TWO TESTS DO MOST OF THE WORK AND THEY MUST BE RUN SEPARATELY. THE NOUN TEST: is the thing named a VIRTUE a pupil IS (respect, integrity, resilience, kindness) or a CONDUCT a pupil DOES (behaviour, manners, uniform, attendance, punctuality)? THE VERB TEST: is that conduct DEMANDED of pupils, or merely valued by the school and claimed about it? Answer each question below on its own evidence and do not let a strong answer to one carry another.

\paragraph{The questions}
\begin{enumerate}\small
\item \textit{any expectation of pupils expressed.} Does the site say ANYTHING AT ALL about how pupils should be or should behave? THE BAR HERE IS DELIBERATELY VERY LOW and most sites will answer true. A values list naming respect or responsibility is enough. A mission statement about the kind of young people the school wants to form is enough. A single sentence about behaviour, manners, uniform or attendance is enough. It counts inside a strapline, an acronym, a head's welcome or a vision statement. Answer FALSE only where the crawl genuinely never addresses this --- where it is curriculum, results, facilities, admissions, term dates and news, and an adult reading it would learn nothing about what is expected of pupils. That is a real kind of school website and it must be recorded rather than read generously --- but it is UNCOMMON, measured at 3 of 50 on this corpus. Do not reach for FALSE merely because a site's conduct language is thin.
\item \textit{conduct noun named not just a virtue.} Does the site name CONDUCT ITSELF --- behaviour, manners, uniform, attendance, punctuality, discipline --- as something the school cares about? THIS IS THE NOUN TEST AND IT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT QUESTION HERE. A VIRTUE is a quality a pupil IS: respect, integrity, responsibility, resilience, kindness, courage, ambition, scholarship. A CONDUCT is something a pupil DOES. ``High standards of behaviour'', ``we are proud of our pupils'' manners', ``good attendance matters'' all name conduct and answer TRUE. ``We expect pupils to show integrity'', ``our values are respect, resilience and responsibility'', ``we want pupils to be kind'' name virtues and answer FALSE --- AND THEY ANSWER FALSE EVEN WHEN A DEMAND VERB IS ATTACHED. Check the NOUN, never the verb. Note that ``respect'' can go either way and you must read which is meant: ``respect'' in a values list is a virtue; ``pupils speak respectfully to staff'' is conduct. THE NOUN MUST APPEAR IN A SENTENCE. A conduct noun standing alone as a page heading, a menu label, a bullet in a list of topics, or an item in a values acronym --- ``Behaviour'', ``Uniform'', ``Attendance'' --- is the site naming a TOPIC it has a page about, not saying that it cares about that conduct. Answer FALSE unless the school has written a sentence containing the noun.
\item \textit{climate word applied to the school.} In a SENTENCE OF PROSE, does the site describe the SCHOOL, its classrooms or its corridors as having an ORDERLY WORKING ATMOSPHERE, using a word from this list or a close neighbour of one? CALM, ORDERLY, PURPOSEFUL, SETTLED, FOCUSED, DISCIPLINED, STRUCTURED, WELL-ORDERED, INDUSTRIOUS, HARMONIOUS. Check against that printed list rather than judging a phrase fresh. ``A calm and purposeful learning environment'', ``an orderly and settled school'', ``classrooms are focused and industrious'' all answer TRUE. It does not matter how many such words are strung together --- a chain of them is still one finding. FOUR WORDS ARE DELIBERATELY NOT ON THE LIST AND DO NOT COUNT ON THEIR OWN. ``SAFE'' and ``SECURE'' are safeguarding and pastoral care, not a working atmosphere, and they are the commonest way this question is answered wrongly --- ``a safe and happy place to learn'' answers FALSE. ``RESPECTFUL'' on its own is a virtue claim and belongs to the noun test. ``POSITIVE'' and ``HAPPY'' are generic marketing language that nearly every school website uses. Any of these four counts ONLY when it sits in the same phrase as a word that IS on the printed list --- ``a safe, calm and orderly school'' answers TRUE because of ``calm and orderly''. IT MUST BE A SENTENCE THE SCHOOL HAS WRITTEN. A strapline, a banner, an acronym, a values list, a page heading or a three-word tagline is not a description of the environment and answers FALSE. WHO THE SENTENCE IS ABOUT DECIDES. This question is about the ENVIRONMENT. If the same word is aimed at pupils as something they must do --- ``we expect pupils to move calmly and quietly between lessons'' --- that is a demand and belongs to the demand questions below, not here.
\item \textit{conduct demanded of pupils.} Is CONDUCT stated as something the school DEMANDS of pupils, rather than something it values or claims to have? The test is a verb of demand aimed at pupils --- expect, require, insist, must, will, non-negotiable --- AND the thing demanded must be a CONDUCT. ``We expect pupils to arrive on time and in full uniform'' answers TRUE. ``Pupils must wear the school uniform'' answers TRUE. ANSWER FALSE WHERE THE DEMAND VERB IS ATTACHED TO A BARE VIRTUE. ``We expect pupils to show integrity'', ``students are expected to be hopeful, charitable and scholarly'', ``we expect all our community to demonstrate Integrity, Responsibility and Resilience'' are demands about what a pupil should BE, and they answer FALSE. This is the single most common misreading of this instrument. Also FALSE: a claim that the school HAS good behaviour, which is a description and not a demand; academic expectation, however forcefully stated; a demand governing staff, parents or visitors' own conduct.
\item \textit{first person collective conduct norm.} Does the site publish a conduct standard IN THE FIRST PERSON PLURAL --- ``we arrive on time, in the correct uniform, ready to learn'', ``we listen when others are speaking'', ``we walk on the left'', ``we look after our school''? THIS IS A DEMAND, NOT A DESCRIPTION OF WHAT HAPPENS. It is the school publishing a standard its pupils are held to, in the voice it uses to hold them; the absence of ``must'' or ``expect'' is a house style, not a weaker claim. ``We arrive on time'' is a standard, not a report about yesterday. TWO GUARDS, BOTH OF WHICH RUN FIRST. (a) THE NOUN TEST STILL DECIDES: a first-person norm naming only virtues --- ``we are respectful'', ``we show kindness'', ``we treat each other with respect'' --- answers FALSE, exactly as any other bare virtue would. (b) A first-person statement about the SCHOOL rather than about pupil acts --- ``we are a calm and purposeful school'', ``we pride ourselves on excellent behaviour'' --- is a climate claim and answers FALSE.
\item \textit{code of conduct referred to as binding.} Does the site refer to a code of conduct, a set of rules, a behaviour curriculum or a charter AS SOMETHING THAT BINDS PUPILS --- in its own prose? Answer true where the school says such a thing exists and applies: ``all pupils follow our code of conduct'', ``our behaviour curriculum sets out what is expected in every lesson'', ``the school rules apply at all times''. ANSWER FALSE FOR NAVIGATION FURNITURE AND LINKS. A menu item reading ``Behaviour Policy'', a breadcrumb, a sidebar list, a bare page heading, or the title of a downloadable document is a pointer to a page and not a statement the school has made. A LINK IS NOT A STATEMENT. Also FALSE where a policy is merely available for download, or where the rules named govern staff, parents or visitors.
\item \textit{small particular of conduct named.} Does the site name a SMALL PARTICULAR of conduct --- going down a level rather than naming the level? What qualifies: uniform specifics (a blazer, a tie, skirt length, no trainers); equipment a pupil must bring; a rule about phones; arriving by a stated time; a named corridor or classroom routine (line up, walk on the left, stand when an adult enters, tracking the speaker); a named standard of dress or conduct given in detail. A DOMAIN NAMED IS NOT A PARTICULAR, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE QUESTION. ``Clear expectations around attendance, absence and punctuality'' and ``personal appearance, great attendance, good manners --- our non-negotiables'' name the AREAS without saying anything small, and they answer FALSE. ``On time, in the correct uniform and with the correct equipment'' specifies, and answers TRUE. The construct is granularity: the site has to go down a level, not list the levels.
\item \textit{named consequence stated.} Does the site NAME what follows when a pupil does not meet an expectation? A named response answers TRUE: a detention, a warning, being sent somewhere, a call home, a removal from the lesson, a described restorative conversation. A CONSEQUENCE MUST BE NAMED, NOT REFERRED TO. ``Sanctions exist and are acted upon'', ``pupils understand there are consequences if rules are broken'', ``we follow up on poor behaviour'' assert that something follows without saying what, and they answer FALSE. A REWARD IS NOT A CONSEQUENCE for this question --- house points and certificates are recognition of good conduct, not what follows a failure to meet the standard.
\item \textit{neg demand attached only to virtues.} Is EVERY demand the site makes of pupils attached to a virtue rather than to a conduct? Answer true where the site does use demand language --- expect, require, must --- but everything it demands is a quality a pupil should BE: ``we expect all students to respect and support our values'', ``students are expected to be hopeful, charitable and scholarly'', ``we expect our community to demonstrate Integrity, Responsibility, Resilience'', and nowhere does it demand anything a pupil DOES. Answer FALSE as soon as the site demands one conduct anywhere in the crawl, and answer FALSE where the site makes no demands at all --- that is a different finding. This question is identifying specifically the site that SOUNDS demanding because of its verbs while requiring nothing but character.
\item \textit{neg only academic expectation.} Is all of the site's ``expectation'' language academic rather than about conduct? Answer true where the site speaks of high expectations, aspiration, excellence, challenge, ambition or ``the best from every pupil'', and nowhere in the crawl attaches an expectation to behaviour, manners, uniform, attendance or punctuality. Answer FALSE as soon as one expectation is attached to conduct, and FALSE where the site uses no expectation language at all. If the site does not say which kind of expectation it means, treat it as academic --- that is the ladder's rule.
\item \textit{neg conduct words only in nav furniture.} Does the site's conduct vocabulary appear ONLY in navigation furniture and never in prose? Answer true where words like ``Uniform'', ``Attendance'', ``Behaviour Policy'', ``Code of Conduct'' or ``Rewards and Sanctions'' appear as menu labels, breadcrumbs, sidebar items, bare headings or the titles of downloadable documents, and the crawl contains no sentence in which the school itself says anything about conduct. Answer FALSE as soon as there is one such sentence anywhere, however brief, and FALSE where there is no conduct vocabulary at all. A heading followed by a sentence is prose, not furniture.
\item \textit{neg conduct language confined to a values list.} Is EVERYTHING the site says about how pupils should be confined to a values list, a strapline, a motto or an acronym --- with no ordinary sentence developing any of it? THIS IS A POSITIVE FINDING ABOUT A REAL AND COMMON KIND OF SCHOOL WEBSITE, not a residue. Answer true where the crawl gives you ``Respect $\cdot$ Resilience $\cdot$ Responsibility'', a CARE or ASPIRE acronym with each letter expanded to a single word, or a banner reading ``Be Kind, Work Hard, Aim High'', and the school never goes on to say anything further about conduct or character in prose. Answer FALSE as soon as ONE ordinary sentence develops the point --- ``we expect pupils to show respect by listening when others speak'', or any sentence at all about behaviour, uniform, attendance or manners. Answer FALSE where the site has no values language at all; that is a different finding, recorded by the floor question. A list that is merely LONG is still a list. What ends this finding is a SENTENCE, not more items.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{The banding rule}
A site that expresses no expectation of pupils is band 1; a virtue without a conduct is band 2; a named conduct is band 3; conduct demanded of pupils is band 4. Negative findings (demands attached only to virtues, purely academic expectations, conduct words only in navigation or a values list) cap the band unless the site has specified particulars. A five-band variant used for scale consistency adds band 5 where the site both names a small particular of conduct and states a consequence; this fires for 25 schools nationally.

The instrument additionally carries 13 exclusion clauses and 8 hard rules, stated in full in \texttt{score\_website\_strictness\_v13.py}.

\subsection*{Interview strictness}

Prompt version \texttt{interview-strictness-v13-sequence-not-location}. Construct:
You are reading a headteacher's account of how behaviour is handled in their school. Nearly all of them will say that a behaviour system exists, so the existence of one separates almost nobody. Two things do separate them. The first is DETAIL: whether the headteacher actually takes you through how the system runs inside a lesson --- the steps, in order, starting with what happens in the room --- or only names it and moves on. The second is what the headteacher chooses to say ABOUT conduct: whether they claim a high standard of behaviour is expected and consistently held, and whether they say the school goes after small things, applies immediate consequences, or requires a standard way of sitting, listening and moving about. You are describing what the headteacher SAYS. You are not judging whether the school is strict, whether the regime is a good one, or whether the headteacher is right.

\paragraph{The questions}
\begin{enumerate}\small
\item \textit{escalating sanction system.} Does the headteacher indicate that their school has a behaviour system in which consequences ESCALATE --- where one thing follows another if the behaviour continues or recurs? Qualifying: a named ladder or staged policy; a points or tally arrangement where reaching a threshold brings a further consequence; a sequence running from a first response through detention, removal, internal exclusion or suspension. The escalation may be described in a single sentence --- this question is only about whether such a system is there. This is a LOW bar and nearly every headteacher clears it. Its only job is to tell an interview that reached behaviour apart from one that did not, and it can never lift a school on its own.
\item \textit{classroom level walkthrough.} Does the headteacher SET OUT THE SEQUENCE OF DISTINCT RESPONSES a pupil meets as misbehaviour continues --- what happens first, and what happens next if it does not stop? Qualifying, DESCRIBED rather than quoted so that none of this wording can be handed back as evidence: the head names two or more responses of DIFFERENT KINDS in order --- a spoken reminder and then a recorded warning; a warning and then removal to a named place; a coded step and then the step above it. A step may be named by a code, by what the adult does, or by where the pupil goes. THE HEADTEACHER DOES NOT HAVE TO SAY WHERE ANY STEP HAPPENS: an ordered ladder of distinct responses answers this question whether or not the words lesson, classroom or room are ever used. THESE FAIL AND MUST RETURN FALSE: a policy described by its PROPERTIES rather than its steps --- that it is graduated, clear, numerical, co-constructed, shared with parents or displayed in classrooms; a running TALLY of points or merits with no distinct responses named, because accumulating points is one mechanism and not a sequence; ONE sanction whose SIZE increases --- a detention that simply runs longer each time it is repeated is a single response getting bigger, not a sequence of different responses; an INVENTORY of the powers a school holds --- detention, internal exclusion, suspension, managed move --- listed as things that are available rather than as what follows what; and a head who names a step or two and then declines to go through it, offering to send the detail separately or waving it off as the usual arrangement. THE TEST: from what the headteacher has said, could you name the first response and the DIFFERENT response that follows it? IF IN DOUBT, ANSWER FALSE.
\item \textit{behaviour expectations high.} Does the headteacher CLAIM that this school expects a high standard of BEHAVIOUR --- that conduct is demanded and treated as central, not hoped for? THIS QUESTION IS ABOUT THE CLAIM, NOT ABOUT ANY PARTICULAR WORDS. A headteacher can make it without ever saying ``expectations'': saying that behaviour is the first thing everything else is built on, or that a disruption-free lesson is what the school is organised around, or that conduct is the single most important thing in a school, is this claim stated plainly. Equally, the words can be present and the claim absent. THESE FAIL AND MUST RETURN FALSE: high expectations of ACADEMIC work, aspiration, ambition, outcomes or achievement, which are a different dimension and are the commonest wrong answer here; a warm statement that the pupils are wonderfully behaved, which is a compliment about pupils and not a demand made of them; the mere existence of a sanction system, which is machinery and is asked about separately. IF IN DOUBT, ANSWER FALSE.
\item \textit{consistency of behaviour.} Does the headteacher CLAIM that behaviour, or the expectations attached to it, are applied CONSISTENTLY across the school --- that pupils meet the same response from every adult? Qualifying, DESCRIBED rather than quoted: the head says staff hold the same line on conduct wherever a pupil goes; or that the behaviour expectations are applied the same way by everyone; or that consistency in how behaviour is handled is what makes the school work. THESE FAIL AND MUST RETURN FALSE, and between them they are the majority of the times this word appears: consistency of anything other than conduct --- of values, of teaching, of curriculum, of culture in general; and any sentence in which the headteacher is CONCEDING that consistency is not yet there, which includes naming it as an area for growth, putting a percentage on it short of complete, or saying it will never be total. A headteacher describing what they are working towards has not made this claim. IF IN DOUBT, ANSWER FALSE.
\item \textit{small stuff pursued.} Does the headteacher CLAIM that the school deliberately goes after SMALL MISBEHAVIOUR IN LESSONS --- that low-level disruption is picked up rather than let go? Qualifying, DESCRIBED rather than quoted: the head says the school is attentive to minor disruption and that nothing small is allowed to pass; or names the kind of small in-lesson conduct that gets a response, such as calling out, talking over the teacher, turning round, or not attending while someone is explaining; or says explicitly that dealing with the small things is how the serious things are prevented. THESE FAIL AND MUST RETURN FALSE. First, and this is the commonest wrong answer: A TARIFF LIST --- the things that earn a detention, set out as a list, whatever happens to be on it. Lateness, missing homework, missing equipment, chewing gum, and above all uniform, ties and skirts, which Damian ruled is not small stuff in classroom-behaviour terms. Nearly every school has such a list, so it separates nobody, and setting a detention for something minor is not the same as CLAIMING that the school goes after the small things. This question is looking for the claim, not the tariff. Second, an account only of what happens after serious incidents. Third --- and this is the one that catches most often --- small things named in a DENIAL or a DIAGNOSIS rather than a practice, where the head is saying the school does not operate that way, or is describing little things accumulating into disorder as a problem they have. IF IN DOUBT, ANSWER FALSE.
\item \textit{instant consequences.} Does the headteacher say that certain behaviours bring an IMMEDIATE and AUTOMATIC consequence --- that for some things there is no warning, no discussion and no discretion, the consequence simply follows? Qualifying, DESCRIBED rather than quoted: the head names a behaviour that goes straight to a consequence with nothing in between; or says the school has a very low tolerance of a named kind of conduct and that something follows at once; or describes a consequence as automatic once the behaviour has happened. THESE FAIL AND MUST RETURN FALSE: an escalating ladder in which a warning comes first, which is the ordinary case and is asked about separately; a consequence described as quick or well-organised rather than automatic; a statement that the school responds firmly, with no behaviour named. IF IN DOUBT, ANSWER FALSE.
\item \textit{default comportment.} Does the headteacher name a required DEFAULT WAY OF CONDUCTING ONESELF that pupils are expected to adopt as standard --- a prescribed posture, a way of attending to the teacher, or a way of moving around the building? Qualifying: a named acronym or routine of the SLANT type; a stated requirement about how pupils sit or where they look while someone is speaking; silent or single-file transitions; lining up or entering the room in a specified way; a standard start-of-lesson routine that pupils perform. YOU MUST BE ABLE TO SAY WHAT THE PUPIL IS REQUIRED TO DO. THESE FAIL AND MUST RETURN FALSE: a general statement that the school is calm, orderly or purposeful, which describes an outcome rather than a required comportment; a general reference to the school having routines, or being structured, or being consistent about routines, where no routine is named and nothing is said about what it requires of a pupil; uniform and equipment; and any such routine named in a DENIAL, where the headteacher is saying their school does NOT do that --- a head who says they do not have silent corridors has not named a default comportment, they have rejected one. IF IN DOUBT, ANSWER FALSE.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{The banding rule}
\begin{description}
\item[Band 1] No escalating sanction system is discussed.
\item[Band 2] An escalating system is mentioned, but the headteacher does not set out the sequence of distinct responses it puts a pupil through.
\item[Band 3] The escalating system AND the sequence of distinct responses. Where most headteachers belong.
\item[Band 4] All of 3, plus high expectations of behaviour or consistency of behaviour.
\item[Band 5] All of 3, plus sweating the small stuff, instant consequences, or a default comportment. Band-4 material is not required --- see derive\_band.
\end{description}

The instrument additionally carries 8 exclusion clauses and 7 hard rules, stated in full in \texttt{score\_interview\_strictness.py}.

\subsection*{Interview teaching}

Prompt version \texttt{interview-teaching-v3-scope-of-the-practice-account}. Construct:
You are reading a headteacher's account of teaching, feedback and assessment in their school --- what makes a teacher effective, how marking and feedback work, and how pupil progress is assessed. Almost every headteacher will say something about all three, so having an answer separates nobody. What separates them is HOW MUCH OF THE SCHOOL'S PRACTICE THEY ACCOUNT FOR: how many distinct parts of it they can describe --- what good teaching consists of, how it is done, how feedback reaches pupils, how progress is measured, what is done about the gaps it finds --- and whether they reach the demanding end, where the school has one shared way of teaching, names the evidence behind it, or closes the loop from assessment back to what is taught again. Answer each question independently about what the headteacher SAYS. You are not judging whether the teaching is good, whether the approach is the right one, or whether the headteacher is right.

\paragraph{The questions}
\begin{enumerate}\small
\item \textit{teaching or assessment is discussed.} Does the headteacher say anything at all about teaching, marking, feedback or assessment in their school? This is a very low bar and nearly every headteacher clears it. Its only job is to tell an interview that reached the subject apart from one that went elsewhere. It can never lift a school on its own.
\item \textit{a feedback practice named.} Does the headteacher name HOW feedback reaches pupils in their school? Qualifying: a whole-school marking or feedback policy; a stated frequency or expectation for marking; a named code, symbol set or coloured-pen arrangement; time set aside for pupils to respond to feedback; verbal or live feedback named as the method. Something about the mechanism must be said. A statement that teachers give good feedback, with no arrangement described, does NOT qualify.
\item \textit{teacher qualities named.} Does the headteacher name a QUALITY that makes a teacher effective, other than their relationships with pupils? Qualifying: subject knowledge or expertise; passion, enthusiasm or love of the subject; the ability to explain; being well organised or well prepared; high expectations of pupils' work; reflectiveness or willingness to improve; resilience. THIS FAILS: relationships with pupils, which is asked separately; and behaviour management, which this rubric does not score.
\item \textit{formative assessment described.} Does the headteacher describe assessment used to FIND OUT WHAT PUPILS HAVE NOT UNDERSTOOD, as distinct from recording how they did? Qualifying: assessment for learning or formative assessment named as such; low-stakes quizzing to find gaps; exit tickets; checking for misconceptions; mini-assessments whose purpose is diagnosis; the head saying assessment is there to tell teachers what to do next. THIS FAILS: tests and mocks described only as measurement, which are asked about separately.
\item \textit{pupil progress is tracked.} Does the headteacher describe an arrangement for TRACKING pupil progress across the school? Qualifying: data drops, data capture or assessment points at stated intervals; a named tracking or reporting system; predicted grades, target grades or flight paths; progress compared against a benchmark; reports to parents at stated points. THIS FAILS: a single mention of exam results with no tracking arrangement described.
\item \textit{feedback method beyond written marking.} Does the headteacher name a feedback method OTHER than a teacher writing in a pupil's book? Qualifying: whole-class feedback; live or in-the-moment marking during a lesson; verbal feedback named as the school's method; use of a visualiser to model work; peer or self-assessment against a mark scheme; modelled answers worked through with the class. THIS FAILS: written marking described as being done more efficiently, and a policy that only says how often books are marked.
\item \textit{relationships named as teacher quality.} Does the headteacher name RELATIONSHIPS WITH PUPILS, or rapport, among the things that make a teacher effective? The relationship must be offered as part of what makes the teaching work. THIS FAILS: relationships described as part of the school's pastoral care rather than as a teaching quality, and relationships between staff.
\item \textit{explicit instruction described.} Does the headteacher describe teaching in which the TEACHER SHOWS PUPILS HOW before they do it themselves? Qualifying: modelling, worked examples, teacher explanation named as the core of the lesson, scaffolding that is gradually removed, breaking learning into steps, a stated sequence in which the teacher demonstrates and then the class practises, direct or explicit instruction named as such. THIS FAILS: a general statement that lessons are well structured or well planned.
\item \textit{adaptive teaching described.} Does the headteacher describe teaching being ADAPTED to different pupils within a class? Qualifying: differentiation or adaptive teaching named; scaffolding for pupils who need it; stretch or challenge for the highest attainers; adjustments for pupils with SEND described as a teaching practice; the head saying teachers change what they do to suit the particular class. THIS FAILS: setting, streaming or ability grouping, which is a timetabling arrangement rather than a teaching one; and separate intervention groups outside lessons.
\item \textit{questioning technique named.} Does the headteacher name a QUESTIONING OR CHECKING technique teachers use? Qualifying: cold calling or a no-hands-up arrangement; mini-whiteboards; a named way of checking the whole class has understood before moving on; targeted or planned questioning; think-pair-share; a hinge question. THIS FAILS: a general statement that teachers ask good questions, with no technique named.
\item \textit{retrieval or memory practice named.} Does the headteacher describe practice aimed at making pupils REMEMBER over time? Qualifying: retrieval practice; recall or knowledge starters; a do-now or settler whose purpose is recall; low-stakes quizzing on earlier content; knowledge organisers; spaced or interleaved practice; the head talking about long-term memory or about knowledge sticking. THIS FAILS: revision for an imminent exam, which is preparation rather than a memory practice.
\item \textit{summative assessment arrangement described.} Does the headteacher describe a formal ASSESSMENT ARRANGEMENT for measuring what pupils have learned? Qualifying: mocks or trial exams at stated points; end-of-unit, end-of-term or end-of-year assessments as a school-wide arrangement; standardised or common assessments across a year group; past papers used as an assessment rather than as revision. Something about the arrangement must be described. THIS FAILS: a mention of GCSEs or public examinations as an event the school prepares for.
\item \textit{marking workload addressed.} Does the headteacher say the school has DELIBERATELY LIMITED what teachers are asked to mark, or changed the arrangement to make it sustainable? Qualifying: a stated decision not to mark every piece; marking reduced, simplified or replaced with something quicker; workload named as the reason for how the policy is written; the head saying deep marking was stopped. THIS FAILS: a general statement that staff workload matters, with nothing said about marking or feedback.
\item \textit{research or evidence base named.} Does the headteacher name the RESEARCH OR EVIDENCE the school's teaching approach rests on? Qualifying: a named researcher, author or framework --- Rosenshine, Wiliam, Sherrington, Lemov, cognitive science, cognitive load theory, the Education Endowment Foundation, a named piece of guidance the school works to. YOU MUST BE ABLE TO NAME WHAT IS BEING CITED. THIS FAILS: a general statement that the school is research-informed or evidence-based with nothing named.
\item \textit{a shared teaching model is school wide.} Does the headteacher say the school has ONE AGREED WAY OF TEACHING that all teachers follow? Qualifying: a named lesson structure, teaching framework or set of non-negotiables that every lesson uses; a stated expectation that a visitor would see the same shape in any classroom; a school-wide pedagogy the head can describe. THIS FAILS: a whole-school MARKING policy, which is asked about separately; and a statement that teachers are free to teach in their own way, which is the opposite of this claim.
\item \textit{assessment leads to reteaching.} Does the headteacher close the loop --- say what HAPPENS to what assessment finds? Qualifying: content being retaught or revisited because an assessment showed it had not landed; gap analysis feeding into what is planned next; the curriculum or scheme of work changed in response to assessment; the head saying assessment is pointless unless it changes the next lesson. THIS FAILS: assessment results being reported to parents or to leaders, and pupils being placed in an intervention group, neither of which is a change to what is taught.
\item \textit{neg practice left to departments.} Does the headteacher say there is NO whole-school approach --- that marking, feedback or teaching method is left to individual departments or individual teachers to decide? Qualifying: the head says there is no single policy; or that each subject does it their own way and that is deliberate; or that they do not prescribe how teachers teach. THIS FAILS: a whole-school framework that departments then apply in a subject-appropriate way, which is a shared approach rather than the absence of one.
\item \textit{neg practice conceded inconsistent.} Does the headteacher CONCEDE that the practice they are describing is not yet happening reliably? Qualifying: the head says it is inconsistent, or variable, or patchy; that it happens in some subjects and not others; that it is an area for development or something they are working on; that compliance is short of complete. THIS FAILS: a description of how much better it is than it used to be, where the head also states that it is now in place.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{The banding rule}
\begin{description}
\item[Band 1] The interview barely reaches teaching or assessment.
\item[Band 2] Teaching is discussed but little of the practice is accounted for, or the head says there is no whole-school approach.
\item[Band 3] An ordinary account: what makes a teacher good, and how feedback and assessment work. Where most headteachers belong.
\item[Band 4] A broad account covering many distinct parts of the school's practice.
\item[Band 5] A broad account that also reaches the demanding end --- one shared way of teaching, a named evidence base, or assessment that changes what is taught.
\end{description}

The instrument additionally carries 7 exclusion clauses and 7 hard rules, stated in full in \texttt{score\_interview\_teaching\_v3.py}.

\subsection*{Interview warmth (counted statements)}

Prompt version \texttt{interview-warmth-prose-v1-counted-relational-statements}.
This instrument gives the model a short written rubric and asks it to
count, with verbatim quotations, the relational statements in the
headteacher's answers (statements placing staff and pupils in relation)
and the subset that name a concrete mechanism. The band the model
offers is discarded; the reported band is recomputed in code from the
verified counts. The pre-registered rubric is
\texttt{RUBRIC\_interview\_warmth\_prose\_v1.md} in the repository.

\subsection*{Website identity (faith prominence)}

A three-way classifier (teaching philosophy, religious character,
faith prominence) reads the same crawl text and returns categorical
judgements; faith prominence is graded none, incidental, present or
central. This instrument is retained on the older model it was
validated with (\cref{sec:p1_scoring_lessons}); its full rubric is in
\texttt{analyse\_website\_scores.py}.
